Virtuously
VUR-choo-us-lee
adv. (in a manner marked by moral excellence; with the strength of character Scripture commends in a woman of worth)
From virtue, Latin virtus, moral strength or worth, originally bound up with vir, a man, broadened to name moral excellence generally, + the adverbial -ly.

Biblical Definition

Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.

This is the closing verdict of the acrostic poem on the woman who feareth the LORD in Proverbs 31, spoken by her husband and children in the gate where public reputation is weighed. Virtuously here is not decorative praise but a summary of the whole preceding portrait — she rises before dawn, works with willing hands, considers a field and buys it, stretches out her hand to the needy, clothes her household in scarlet, and opens her mouth with wisdom. Her excellence is not passive ornamentation but vigorous, skillful, God-fearing labor exercised within her household under her husband's headship, and it is precisely this combination — strength, industry, wisdom, and the fear of the LORD — that the text calls virtue in a woman. The comparison many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all does not diminish other virtuous women; it crowns this one as the model toward which the praise of all others points. The chapter closes where it should: her own works praise her in the gates, a public honor earned by private faithfulness, not claimed by self-promotion.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from VIRTUE: moral goodness; strength of character; conformity of life and conduct to the moral law.

expand to see more

VIRTUE, n. Moral goodness; the practice of moral duties, and the abstaining from vice.

VIRTUOUSLY, adv. In a manner marked by moral excellence and strength of character.

Proverbs 31:29 crowns the woman who feareth the LORD as the one who excels all who have done virtuously.

Her virtue is industrious and wise, not merely decorative or passive.

Public honor in the gates follows private, God-fearing faithfulness in the home.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:29 — "Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all."

Modern Corruption

Modern secular feminism redefines a woman's worth by autonomous self-actualization and career achievement detached from the home, household, and the fear of the LORD that Proverbs 31 actually commends.

expand to see more

Second-wave and later feminist thought recast female excellence as self-defined achievement outside the household, often treating domestic industry as confinement rather than, as Proverbs 31 presents it, a field of vigorous strength, skill, and wisdom exercised under God.

Scripture's portrait does not oppose capability to domesticity; the virtuous woman buys fields, trades profitably, and clothes her household in fine linen, all while her heart's center is the fear of the LORD and her household's good, not autonomous self-definition apart from it. Recovering virtuously means recovering both halves at once: real strength and skill, ordered toward God and household rather than against them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin virtus, moral strength, virtue names moral excellence; virtuously describes conduct exhibiting it, crowned in Proverbs 31 as the fear of the LORD made industrious.

expand to see more

Virtus, Latin for moral strength, underlies virtue.

Virtuously names conduct exhibiting that strength, not mere decoration.

Proverbs 31:29 crowns the woman who feareth the LORD above all others so described.

Her virtue is industrious, skillful, and generous, not passive.

Public honor in the gates follows from private, God-fearing faithfulness.

Usage

"names industrious, wise, God-fearing strength of character, not mere ornament"
